Reddit post, r/houseplants.
Title: Can I recover my plants

Hello, For a couple of weeks my plants started looking like this: leaves drooping and shrinking or curling. I tried not to overwater them. I do it like once pr every two weeks, by checking the soil. We did have some very extreme cold temperatures for weeks with very dry air. I live in Finland and I have my thanksgiving cactus since I moved here, I don’t want to lose it :(. Is there any way I can still save them?

But the soil feels moist :( and already a plant died because of overwatering :(

What is wrong with my plant?
answer:
**Most likely cause: cold stress and root damage from wet soil.** This is a Thanksgiving cactus (*Schlumbergera truncata*). The wrinkled, limp segments in your photos, with soil that still feels moist after two weeks, fit root damage better than thirst. A plant sitting in soggy soil can look almost identical because waterlogged roots lose their ability to function, leaving the stems just as water-starved even when the mix is soaking wet. Cold makes this worse: temperatures below 45°F (7°C) carry a cold damage risk. Cold soil dries slowly, so the roots stay wet longer. Your window and the dry winter air add stress.

**Check first:** Lift the pot and empty any water from the saucer. Then gently slide the plant out. Healthy roots are firm and light-colored, ranging from white to tan. Dark, mushy roots point to rot. Also check the base of the segments at soil level for black or soft spots.

**What to do:**
1. **Stop watering and move it away from cold glass and drafts.** Water again only when the top inch is dry.
2. **If roots are mushy, trim them with clean scissors.** Let the plant sit for 24-48 hours so the roots can dry out before repotting it in a well-draining mix, in a pot with a drainage hole. Wait a few days before watering.
3. **If the stem base is soft or black,** take healthy cuttings of 2–4 firm segments as a backup. Take healthy cuttings before the damage spreads further.
4. **Check for spider mites:** look for fine webbing between segments, since dry indoor air encourages them.

Recovery can take months, and a plant with extensive rot may not survive. Healthy roots mean there is a good chance.

The purple plant (likely an oxalis) is drooping with folded leaves. It may share the same cause, so check its soil and roots too. A photo of its base and the drainage would help.
